The Spanish American Wars of Independence. From 1808 to 1833, this series of military campaigns and revolutions allowed Spanish American colonies to liberate themselves from European dominion and establish independent republics. The wars began after Napoleon's 1808 invasion of Spain destabilized Spanish authority and emboldened colonists yearning for independence. Sparked by Napoleon's invasion of Spain and the power vacuum it created, visionary military commanders like Simon Bolivar and Jose de San Martin led armies across continents, uniting diverse populations against Spanish colonial rule. Simon Bolivar led revolutions across northern South America, liberating Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia, which was named in his honor. Jose de San Martin commanded the Southern Cone independence, liberating Argentina and Chile, then crossing the Andes to strike at Spanish Peru. Bernardo O'Higgins, son of an Irish-Chilean father, emerged as a key allied commander and first Chief Executive of independent Chile. The wars were ideologically inspired by the American Revolution and Enlightenment republicanism, though they faced geographic, economic, and social barriers the north had not. Spain initially resisted fiercely, deploying experienced troops to crush rebellions, but lacked the resources to reconquer so vast a territory simultaneously. By 1830, Spain retained only Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Americas, a stunning reversal from its prior three centuries of hemispheric dominance. By the 1830s, nearly all of Spanish America had broken free, reshaping the hemispheric political landscape and establishing the nation-states of modern Latin America.
